hints: Focus on electrons as the link, the manganate(VII) gains electrons while both parts of iron(II) ethanedioate lose them.
Work out how many electrons one formula unit of $\text{FeC}_2\text{O}_4$ gives in total, one from $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ plus two from $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$.
Balance total electrons gained by one mole of $\text{MnO}_4^-$ against electrons lost per mole of $\text{FeC}_2\text{O}_4$ to find the mole ratio.
walkthrough:
**See what gains and loses electrons**

Think of this as an electron balancing puzzle. Manganate(VII) is the oxidising agent and each mole takes up 5 electrons.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{MnO}_4^- + 8\text{H}^+ + 5\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Count electrons given out by one FeC2O4**

One mole of $\text{FeC}_2\text{O}_4$ gives one mole of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and one mole of $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$, and both are oxidised. Add their electrons together.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{e}^-$$
$$\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2 + 2\text{e}^-$$
Total per $\text{FeC}_2\text{O}_4 = 1 + 2 = 3$ moles of $\text{e}^-$

**Balance electrons to get the mole ratio**

Electrons lost must equal electrons gained. One mole of manganate needs 5 moles of electrons, each mole of ethanedioate supplies 3.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{moles of FeC}_2\text{O}_4 = \frac{5}{3} = 1.67$$

options.A: This is the upside down ratio, $3/5 = 0.60$. It gives moles of manganate that react with one mole of ethanedioate, not moles of ethanedioate that react with one mole of manganate.
options.B: Correct and well done. Each $\text{FeC}_2\text{O}_4$ supplies 3 electrons in total, while each $\text{MnO}_4^-$ accepts 5 electrons, so $5/3 = 1.67$ moles are needed to balance electrons.
options.C: This uses $5/2 = 2.50$ and counts only the ethanedioate ion. It forgets that $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ also gives one electron per $\text{FeC}_2\text{O}_4$.
options.D: This uses $5/1 = 5.00$ and counts only the iron(II) to iron(III) change. It forgets that $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ to $\text{CO}_2$ gives two more electrons per $\text{FeC}_2\text{O}_4$.
